title: Avoiding Over-Inference
subtitle: Only infer as far as the text supports — don't pull in outside knowledge or extrapolate too far.
quick_ref: Inference works inside the text. The moment you reach for outside knowledge or a conclusion the clues don't support, you've over-inferred. Stay close to the page.
mini_lesson:
**Over-inference is the most common advanced-reader mistake.**

Plateaued readers know inference is important — but they often go TOO FAR. They reach conclusions the text doesn't quite support, usually by leaning on outside knowledge.

**Two forms of over-inference:**

1. **Outside knowledge.** You add information from your own life or general knowledge that the text doesn't give you.
   - Text: *"Mia is a fifth grader who loves to read."*
   - Over-inference: *"Mia probably gets straight A's."*
   - The text doesn't say anything about her grades. "Loves to read" doesn't necessarily mean A's.

2. **Extrapolation beyond the clue.** You take a small clue and stretch it into a much bigger conclusion than the clue supports.
   - Text: *"He frowned at the menu and ordered water."*
   - Over-inference: *"His family is bankrupt and he's about to drop out of school."*
   - The clue supports something — maybe he's not hungry, or not buying. It doesn't support that big a story.

**The test:**

After making an inference, ask:

> Is this the SMALLEST conclusion the clue supports, or am I adding stuff?

The smallest, closest-to-the-text conclusion is usually the right inference. The bigger, more dramatic one is usually over-inference.

**Trap-spotting:**

Wrong-answer choices in test questions often include over-inferences. They sound smart but they go further than the text supports. If you find yourself thinking "well, in real life this would mean...", pull back — that's outside knowledge.

**Rule:**

> Stay one step beyond the text. Not two. Not three.
why_it_matters: Over-inference is the trap that catches advanced readers more than basic ones — basic readers under-infer, but the next level is to infer the RIGHT amount.
common_trap_1: Adding outside knowledge to an inference ("in real life, this would mean...").
common_trap_2: Extrapolating beyond what the clue supports (small clue, big conclusion).
common_trap_3: Picking a dramatic-sounding answer that goes further than the text justifies.
example_1_text: Text: "Mia is a fifth grader who loves to read." Over-inference: "Mia gets straight A's."
example_1_explanation: Loving to read doesn't tell us about grades. The reader added information that isn't in the text.
example_2_text: Text: "He frowned at the menu and ordered water." Over-inference: "His family is bankrupt and he's about to drop out of school."
example_2_explanation: The clue (frown + water order) supports something small (maybe not hungry, maybe saving money). It doesn't support a whole life crisis.
example_3_text: Text: "The grandmother smiled when she saw the photograph." Reasonable inference: "The photograph means something to her."
example_3_answer: Reasonable — small, close to the text.
example_3_explanation: The smile is the clue. The smallest inference is that the photo matters. We don't know WHY yet; further conclusions would be over-inference.
example_4_text: Text: "Tom didn't come to school for three days." Over-inference: "Tom is in serious trouble at home."
example_4_explanation: The text gives one fact (three absences). It doesn't support a specific cause. "Tom may have been sick or had something going on" would be a more defensible inference.
